drapeaux.note: Francis Hordern's sentence is in French (Le Mouvement social, 1990, quoted by Alain Chatriot); no published English translation exists, so it is translated here. The French wording is the quote as given in the French entry.

titre: The 1936 Paid Vacation Law Is Not in the Matignon Accords
accroche: France, June 1936: paid vacations, absent from the Popular Front's platform as from the text of the Matignon Accords, are voted in a few days.
contenu_vulgarise:
Hôtel de Matignon, Paris, 12:40 a.m. on June 8, 1936. Under the chairmanship of Léon Blum, the General Confederation of French Production (the employers' federation) and the CGT sign an agreement that is nonetheless dated June 7. One will look in vain for paid vacations in it.

## What the Accords Contain

The text has seven articles. Articles 1 and 2 provide for collective labor contracts. Article 3 recognizes freedom of opinion and the right to unionize. Article 4 raises real wages, by 15% for the lowest paid to 7% for the highest, without the total payroll of an establishment being allowed to rise by more than 12%. Article 5 requires worker delegates in establishments with more than ten workers. Articles 6 and 7 rule out sanctions for having gone on strike and call for a return to work.

Paid vacations are not there. Nor were they in the electoral platform of the Popular Front, winner of the elections of April 26 and May 3, as the historian Alain Chatriot points out, who says as much of collective contracts.

## A Law Voted Separately

On June 5, Léon Blum, president of the Council, announces on the radio the immediate introduction of bills. They are introduced in the Chamber as early as June 9, prepared in a rush by the Labor Directorate at the ministry. The Chamber adopts the paid vacation law on June 11, 1936, by 563 votes to one according to the parliamentary channel LCP. The Senate, which had often blocked social laws since the turn of the century, votes on June 17 and 18. The law is promulgated on June 20.

Its content is brief: after one year of continuous service in the establishment, a worker, an employee, or an apprentice is entitled to an annual paid leave of at least fifteen days, including a minimum of twelve working days. It covers industry, commerce, the liberal professions, domestic service, and agriculture.

## What Made It Possible

A right absent from the platform and from the contract, voted by more than five hundred deputies, does not come from nowhere. The legal historian Francis Hordern, cited by Chatriot, notes the speed with which the law was drafted, voted, and carried out, but also recalls that there were earlier parliamentary proposals, debates at the International Labour Organization, and a few local or sectoral experiments. According to Hordern, it was the combination of electoral victory and social mobilization that overcame old resistance.

The question this raises goes beyond June 1936: a right that appeared neither in the platform nor in the contract, but is nevertheless obtained, does it owe itself to what people demand, or to what was prepared before anyone demanded it?

citation.texte: What strikes one most when following the genesis of the law of June 20, 1936 on paid vacations is the speed of its drafting, voting, and execution
citation.source: "Genesis and Vote of the Law of June 20, 1936 on Paid Vacations," Le Mouvement social, no. 150, January-March 1990, p. 19, quoted by Alain Chatriot (Fondation Jean-Jaurès, 2016)

carte.punch: The 1936 paid vacations are neither in the Popular Front platform nor in Matignon.
carte.idee: Signed on June 8, 1936, the Matignon Accords say nothing of paid vacations. A bill introduced on June 9 is adopted by the Chamber on the 11th, by the Senate on the 17th and 18th, and promulgated on June 20: fifteen days after one year of service.

quiz.question: What legal path do paid vacations follow in June 1936?
choix: A bill introduced on June 9 and voted separately from the accords
An article of the Matignon Accords made binding by decree
A commitment in the Popular Front's electoral platform, applied after the elections
A collective agreement extended by the state to all of industry
quiz.explication: The seven articles of Matignon say nothing of paid vacations, which were not in the Popular Front's platform either. They go through a bill introduced on June 9, adopted by the Chamber on the 11th and by the Senate on June 17 and 18, with no collective agreement or new accord between the CGT and the employers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Article 4 of the Matignon Accords, signed on June 8, 1936, provide?
choix: A rise in real wages, by 15% for the lowest paid to 7% for the highest
An annual paid leave of fifteen days after one year of service
The forty-hour week in all establishments
Mandatory collective labor contracts across industry
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 4 of the accords raises real wages, by 15% for the lowest paid to 7% for the highest, with a 12% ceiling on an establishment's total payroll. Paid vacations and the forty-hour week are absent from the text of the accords, and collective contracts fall under Articles 1 and 2, not Article 4.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the text say about the Senate and the paid vacation law?
choix: It had often blocked social laws since the turn of the century, but votes on June 17 and 18
It rejects the text once before adopting it on second reading
It did not have to rule, the law being promulgated by decree
It votes the text on the same day as the Chamber, June 11
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the Senate, which had often blocked social laws since the turn of the century, votes on June 17 and 18, 1936. There is no mention of a rejection followed by a second reading, of promulgation by decree without a Senate vote, or of a vote on the same day as the Chamber, which voted on June 11.
